title: Quantum Computing for Beginners
subtitle: Qubits, gates, the Bloch sphere, interference and entanglement with hands-on circuit labs, for curious kids, teens and adults
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A friendly first course on quantum computing with no maths beyond squares and multiplication. Learn bits and qubits, amplitudes and measurement, the X, H, Z and T gates, interference, circuit text, CNOT, entanglement and Bell states, Deutsch and Grover's algorithms, noise and shots, and what quantum computers are really good for. Every chapter has a hands-on lab built on our own Quantum Web Lab (github.com/lucky-edgelord/quantum-web-lab): a mobile-friendly circuit composer with live chances, Inspect view, a friendly console, ASCII and Q text notation, MicroQiskit (a tiny Qiskit that runs offline) and micro OpenQASM. A few short Python labs build the maths in code. The circuit text notation is inspired by Q.js by Stewart Smith (github.com/stewdio/q.js, MIT) and the layout by the IBM Quantum Composer. Includes an intuitive intro to quantum mechanics, an interactive Bloch sphere chapter, a Qiskit chapter and an OpenQASM chapter.

summary: Everything is made of tiny things, and tiny things do not behave like baseballs. Quantum mechanics is the rulebook for the small world of atoms, electrons and light.
Three ideas carry the whole subject. Things come in packets. Before you look, a thing can be a blend of possibilities. And looking changes what you get.
You do not need to believe it blindly. You will test it with a simulated experiment about light and sunglasses, which gives a surprise that normal thinking cannot explain.

items: ELI5. Imagine the tiniest things are like shy kittens. They come in little packets, they can be curled up in two places until you look, and the moment you peek they pick one. Sunglasses show this: two crossed pairs block the light, but slip a third pair in the middle and light comes back.

Now the real words. The packets are called quanta. Curled up in two places is called a wave or superposition. Peeking is called measurement. Quantum mechanics is just the rulebook for things that small.

Try it. Hold two pairs of polarizing sunglasses at right angles and see black. Now picture a third pair at 45 degrees in the middle: light returns. The lab in this chapter lets you do it with virtual filters.
If you remember one thing: tiny things come in packets, spread like waves, and change when you look.

Start with a ball. Roll it and you know where it is and how fast it goes, always. Baseball rules are called classical physics. They work for balls, cars and planets. They fail for the really small, like an electron. (See Figure 1.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.1. A ball has one path. An electron is a cloud of possibilities until you look.

items: Idea one: things come in packets. You cannot pour light out like water. Light comes as little lumps called photons, and energy as small steps. The word quantum just means a packet or a step. You can have one photon or two, never one and a half.

Idea two: tiny things spread like waves. Shoot one electron at a wall with two slits and it does not pick one slit. It goes through like a wave and the two ripples meet on the other side. Over many electrons the screen shows stripes, from ripples adding and cancelling.
Stripes are interference, the same idea you will use for algorithms.

lesson.code:
# two ripples meet; phi is how far out of step they are
import math
for phi in (0, 90, 180):
    brightness = 2 * (1 + math.cos(math.radians(phi)))
    print(phi, 'degrees out of step: brightness', round(brightness, 2))

items: Idea three: looking changes things. If you place a detector at the slits to see which slit the electron used, the stripes vanish. Asking the electron a plain question forces a plain answer, and the blend is gone. That is measurement, and you met it with the qubit.

Now a test you can do with sunglasses. A polarizing filter is a tiny fence. Light that wiggles along the fence gets through, and light that wiggles across is blocked. Two filters crossed at 90 degrees block everything.
Put a third filter at 45 degrees between them, and some light comes back through! Adding a blocker let more light pass.

Normal thinking says that is impossible. Quantum thinking says each filter is a measurement. After the 45 degree filter, the photon is re-set to that direction, so it has a fair chance of passing the last filter. Open the lab and try it. A photon's direction is a perfect real-world qubit.
(See Figure 1.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 1.2. Two crossed filters block all light, yet a third filter between them lets some through.

summary: A normal computer stores everything as bits. A bit is a tiny switch that is either 0 or 1. Photos, games and messages are all long rows of switches.
A quantum computer uses qubits. A qubit can be 0, 1, or a special mix of both until you look at it. Looking at it is called measuring, and it always gives a plain 0 or 1.

This is not magic and it is not faster at everything. It is a different way to compute, and for a few jobs it can be much faster. This course teaches the real ideas, and you will play with a real simulator all the way.

• Energy and light come in packets, called quanta.
• Tiny things act like waves that can add or cancel.

ELI5. A normal computer is a row of light switches, each on or off. A quantum computer has special switches that can be a little of both until you peek, and then they pick one.
Now the real words. A normal switch is a bit: 0 or 1. The special switch is a qubit. Being a little of both is superposition. Peeking is measurement, and the pick is random but follows chances.

Try it. Flip a real coin ten times and count heads. That is a chance. A qubit has chances too, but it also has a hidden direction that coins do not have. Open the lab and press H to make a fair qubit.
If you remember one thing: a bit is a coin lying flat, a qubit is a coin spinning in the air.
Start with a coin. Flip it and it lands heads or tails. Before you look, you do not know which. Chance describes how likely each one is. A fair coin is 50 percent heads and 50 percent tails.
A normal bit is like a coin lying flat: it is definitely heads or definitely tails. You can read it as often as you like and it never changes. Computers are built from billions of these.

A qubit is more like a coin spinning in the air. While it spins it is not heads and not tails, it is a blend. When it lands, which is when you measure, you get one clean answer. The blend only decides the chances. (See Figure 2.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.1. A bit, a coin and a qubit side by side.

items: Here is why people get excited. To describe 3 normal bits you write 3 digits. To describe 3 qubits you need 8 numbers, one for each possible answer. Add one qubit and you double the numbers. 50 qubits already need more numbers than any laptop can store. (See Figure 2.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 2.2. Each extra qubit doubles the numbers you need.

items: A big warning, because the internet gets this wrong. A quantum computer is not trying every answer at once and handing you the best. When you measure you only get one answer. The skill is in arranging things so the right answer becomes the likely one. You will learn how.
Memory trick: A bit lies flat, a qubit spins. Coin on the table is a bit, coin in the air is a qubit. Add a qubit and the list doubles: 2, 4, 8, 16.

summary: A qubit state has two numbers called amplitudes, one for 0 and one for 1. Write the state as (a, b). The state |0> is (1, 0) and |1> is (0, 1).
The chance of seeing 0 is a squared, and the chance of seeing 1 is b squared. This is the Born rule. The chances must add to 1, so the state is always scaled to fit.
Measuring makes the qubit pick one answer using those chances, and afterwards it stays as that answer. The blend is gone. That is why you measure at the end of a circuit.

ELI5. A qubit is a spinning coin. Its two numbers tell you how likely heads or tails is when it lands. You square the numbers to get the chances, and they always add up to one whole.

Now the real words. The two numbers are amplitudes, one for 0 and one for 1. Squaring an amplitude gives a chance. Measurement is the landing. Amplitudes can be negative, chances cannot, which is why we square.
Try it. Take the numbers 0.6 and 0.8. Square them: 0.36 and 0.64. Those are 36 percent and 64 percent and they add to 100. In the lab, press RY and watch the percentages change.
If you remember one thing: amplitude squared is chance, and the chances add to 100 percent.
Every qubit state is described by two amplitudes. Think of them as dials. One dial is for the answer 0 and one for the answer 1. A plain 0 has the first dial full and the second at zero.

To turn amplitudes into chances you square them. If the state is (0.7071, 0.7071), the chance of 0 is 0.7071 times 0.7071, which is about 0.5. The chance of 1 is also 0.5. That is a fair coin flip. This is called the Born rule. (See Figure 3.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 3.1. Square the amplitudes to get the chances.

lesson.code:
a, b = 0.7071, 0.7071
print('chance of 0:', round(a * a, 2))
print('chance of 1:', round(b * b, 2))

items: Why square? Because amplitudes can be negative, and a chance cannot. Squaring makes every answer positive. Later you will see that the sign matters a lot, because amplitudes can cancel each other out.

Now try it yourself. The lab in this chapter is our own composer. Tap the H gate, then tap a square on the wire. The bars show the chances. Then try the Q Console under the circuit: type h 0 and press Go.

When you run shots, each shot is one full measurement. A coin that is 50 percent heads will not give exactly half every time, just like a real coin. More shots give numbers closer to the true chances.
Memory trick: Square it to share it. Square each amplitude to get a chance, and the chances share 100 percent between them.

summary: A gate is a tiny step that changes a qubit. You build a quantum program by lining gates up on a wire, like beads on a string. Time moves left to right.

X flips 0 and 1, like a NOT. H, the Hadamard, turns a plain 0 into a fair blend. Z flips the sign of the 1 amplitude, which you cannot see directly. T is a smaller sign turn, a quarter of a half-turn.
Every gate can be undone, because it is reversible. Doing X twice is a no-op, and doing H twice gets you back where you started. That is one big difference from normal logic gates.

ELI5. Gates are little moves you do to the spinning coin: flip it, spin it fair, or turn its secret direction. Every move can be undone by doing it again or the opposite way.

Now the real words. The flip is the X gate. The fair spin is the H gate, called Hadamard. The secret turn is the Z gate, which changes the sign of one amplitude but not the chances. T is a smaller secret turn.
Try it. In the gate puzzle lab, start from 0 and tap X: you get 1. Tap H instead: you get a fair coin. Tap H twice and you are back at 0.
If you remember one thing: X flips, H blends, Z twists.
X is the easiest gate. It swaps the two amplitudes. A plain 0 becomes a plain 1 and a plain 1 becomes a plain 0. Think of it as a flip switch.

H, called the Hadamard gate, is the star. Give it a plain 0 and it makes an equal blend. Measure that and you get a fair coin flip. In the circuit text you write it as H. This is how you make your first superposition.

Z does not change the chances of a plain 0 or 1, so it looks like nothing happens. What it does is flip the sign of the 1 amplitude. The sign is called phase. You cannot see it directly, but it changes what the next gate does. (See Figure 4.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 4.1. X, H and Z change the amplitudes in different ways.

lesson.code:
# the gates as number pairs
def x(s): return [s[1], s[0]]
def z(s): return [s[0], -s[1]]
r = 0.7071
def h(s): return [r * (s[0] + s[1]), r * (s[0] - s[1])]
print(h([1, 0]))
print(h(h([1, 0])))

items: Look at that last line. H followed by H returns to the start. The second H cancels the first. This is the hint of something deeper that you will meet in the next chapter.
Tip: in the editor each column is one moment in time and each row is one qubit. You can type circuits in the Q Console too: h 0 adds an H on qubit 0, the top wire, in the next free column.

summary: Amplitudes are like waves. Two waves that line up make a bigger wave. Two waves that are opposite cancel out to nothing. Quantum computers use exactly this.
When two paths lead to the same answer, you add their amplitudes first, and then square. Same sign gives a bigger chance, called constructive interference. Opposite signs cancel, called destructive.
That is the whole trick behind quantum speedups: use phases so that wrong answers cancel and the right answer grows. A coin cannot do this, because ordinary chances only add.

ELI5. Waves can team up or cancel, like two kids pushing a swing in time or against each other. Quantum tricks time the pushes so the wrong answers cancel and the right answer swings high.

Now the real words. Pushing in time is constructive interference: amplitudes with the same sign add up. Pushing against is destructive interference: opposite signs cancel. The sign or angle is called phase.
Try it. Put H, then Z, then H on a qubit that starts at 0. The answer is always 1. Take the Z out and the answer is always 0. Same gates, different timing, opposite result.
If you remember one thing: the whole trick of quantum computing is steering phases so wrong answers cancel.
Here is the experiment of the chapter. Start with a plain 0. Apply H to make a blend. Apply H again. The qubit returns to a plain 0 every time. Nothing random happened at all. (See Figure 5.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.1. Waves in step add up. Waves out of step cancel.

items: That is strange. After the first H you had a fair coin. A fair coin flipped by another fair coin should still be random. The reason it is not: the two paths to the answer 1 have opposite signs and cancel, and the two paths to 0 add up.

Now put a Z between the two H gates. Z flips a sign, so now the paths to 0 cancel and the paths to 1 add up. H then Z then H turns a plain 0 into a plain 1 with certainty. The phase is the steering wheel. (See Figure 5.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 5.2. H, Z, H: the routes to 0 cancel and the routes to 1 add up.

lesson.code:
# H, then a phase turn of phi, then H
import math
for phi in (0, 90, 180):
    p1 = math.sin(math.radians(phi) / 2) ** 2
    print(phi, 'degrees gives chance of 1:', round(p1, 2))

items: With a phase of 0 you get 0 percent, with 180 degrees you get 100 percent, and with 90 degrees you get 50 percent. A phase of 180 degrees is exactly a Z gate. The T gate is 45 degrees. Try these in the labs.
This is why quantum computing needs careful design. You cannot just throw gates at a problem. You line up phases so that the wrong answers cancel. The next chapters build real examples.
Memory trick: Same shines, opposite vanishes. Same sign adds up and shines. Opposite sign cancels and vanishes. Add first, then square.

summary: A single qubit can always be drawn as an arrow from the centre of a ball to its surface. This ball is called the Bloch sphere. It turns the two hidden numbers of a qubit into a picture you can hold in your head.
The north pole is a plain 0 and the south pole is a plain 1. The equator holds the fair blends. How far east you are on the globe is the phase. Every gate is just a turn of the globe.
The sphere only works for one qubit at a time. When a qubit is entangled, its arrow shrinks and sits inside the ball, and that shrinking is a way to see entanglement.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Interference: the real power:

ELI5. The Bloch sphere is a little globe for one qubit. The north pole is a plain 0, the south pole is a plain 1, and the middle is the fair blend. Gates just spin the globe, and a qubit that is glued to another one shrinks its arrow towards the middle.

Now the real words. The arrow from the centre is the state. How high it points sets the chance. Which way around it points is the phase. A gate is a turn of the globe about the x, y or z axis. Pole and equator points have names: |0>, |1>, |+>, |->.
Try it. Open the Bloch tab in the lab and press H: the arrow glides from the north pole to the equator. Drag the sphere to look from the side. Press Z and watch it slide round to the far side.
If you remember one thing: top is 0, bottom is 1, height is chance, and round is phase.

Think of a globe. A plain 0 sits on the north pole and a plain 1 sits on the south pole. A qubit is a pin stuck from the centre of the globe through one spot on the surface. That one arrow tells you everything about the qubit.

Height is chance. At the north pole you always measure 0. At the south pole you always measure 1. On the equator, halfway, you get 0 half the time and 1 half the time. The nearer the arrow is to the south, the more likely a 1. (See Figure 6.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 6.1. The Bloch sphere: north pole is 0, south pole is 1, the equator holds the blends.

items: Why do the two poles stand for states that are so different, yet sit only half a world apart? Because the sphere uses half angles. The angle you see on the sphere is double the angle between the amplitudes.
Opposite poles on the globe are 180 degrees apart, while the states 0 and 1 are as different as two states can be.

Here θ (theta) is how far down from the north pole the arrow points, and φ (phi) is how far around the vertical axis. The chance of a 1 is sin(θ/2) squared. This is the same formula you met with H, phase, H.

Next, the phase. Two arrows at the same height have the same chances, but they can point to different longitudes. The four marked points on the equator are |+⟩ (towards you at 0 degrees), |+i⟩ (90 degrees), |−⟩ (180 degrees) and |−i⟩ (270 degrees).
They all give 50/50 when measured, but they are different states, which is why H then Z then H works.

Now the best part: gates are turns. Imagine pushing a skewer through the globe along an axis and spinning it. X is a half turn about the x axis, so it swaps the poles. Z is a half turn about the vertical axis, so it keeps the poles but turns the equator halfway round, flipping the phase.
Y is a half turn about the y axis.

The H gate is a half turn about a slanted skewer that runs between x and z. It sends the north pole to the +x point on the equator, which is the fair blend |+⟩. Do it twice and you are back at the pole: two half turns make a full turn.
S is a quarter turn about the vertical axis, and T is an eighth. RX, RY and RZ are turns by any angle you choose. (See Figure 6.2 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 6.2. Each gate is a turn of the globe.

items: Open the lab and the Bloch tab, then press H. The arrow glides from the north pole down to +x. Drag the sphere to look from any side, or press Top view to see the phase around the circle. The readout below tells you the exact x, y, z numbers.

A last idea. Put two qubits into a Bell pair and look at each one on its own sphere. Each arrow shrinks to nothing, right in the middle of the ball. Neither qubit alone has a direction, because all the information lives in the link between them. A shorter arrow means entanglement.

What the sphere cannot do: it draws one qubit at a time. For two qubits you need the amplitude table, as in Inspect. Still, almost every one-qubit gate you will ever meet is a turn of this globe, and thinking of it that way makes circuits much easier to guess.

summary: Two qubits have four possible answers: 00, 01, 10 and 11. So a two qubit state is four amplitudes. In our composer the left bit is qubit 0, the top wire.
If the qubits are separate, you can build the four amplitudes by multiplying: the tensor product. A, B gives a0 b0, a0 b1, a1 b0 and a1 b1. A state you can build this way is called a product state.
The CNOT gate links two qubits. If the control is 1, it flips the target. If the control is 0, nothing happens. With H plus CNOT you can make states that are not product states.

ELI5. Two coins can be glued so that one flips only when the other shows heads. That glue gate is called CNOT, and it is how coins start talking to each other.

Now the real words. The coin that decides is the control. The coin that may flip is the target. CNOT is short for controlled NOT. With two qubits there are four answers, 00, 01, 10 and 11, and the state needs four amplitudes.
Try it. In the two-qubit lab put an X on qubit 0 so it is 1, then add CNOT from 0 to 1. Both qubits now read 1. Do it without the X and nothing happens, because the control is 0.
If you remember one thing: if the control says 1, the target turns.
One qubit has two answers, 0 and 1. Two qubits have four, written 00, 01, 10 and 11. The first digit is qubit 0. A state needs one amplitude for each, so four numbers. Three qubits would need eight.

If you set two qubits up separately, you can find the combined state by multiplying. Qubit 0 is (a0, a1) and qubit 1 is (b0, b1). The combined amplitudes are a0 times b0, a0 times b1, a1 times b0 and a1 times b1. This is the tensor product.

def tensor(a, b):
    return [a[0]*b[0], a[0]*b[1], a[1]*b[0], a[1]*b[1]]
print(tensor([1, 0], [0, 1]))   # 0 and 1 gives 01
print(tensor([0.7071, 0.7071], [1, 0]))

summary: Entanglement is when qubits are linked so tightly that you cannot describe one without the others. The famous recipe: put H on qubit 0, then a CNOT from 0 to 1.
The result is the Bell state. It is half 00 and half 11. Measure it and you get 00 or 11, each 50 percent of the time, never 01 or 10. Each qubit alone is a fair coin, but the two coins always agree.
Entanglement does not send messages faster than light. The results look random to each side. You only see the link when you compare them afterwards.

ELI5. Two magic coins can always agree even though each one alone is random, like twins who always pick the same ice cream without talking. That is entanglement, but it cannot be used as a phone.

Now the real words. The recipe is H on one qubit and then CNOT to the other. The result is a Bell state: half 00 and half 11. Each qubit alone is a fair coin, but together they always match. Measuring one tells you the other, but you cannot send a message that way.
Try it. Build the Bell pair in the lab and run 1000 shots. You will see only 00 and 11, about half each, and never 01 or 10. Then open the Bloch tab: each qubit's arrow shrinks to the centre.
If you remember one thing: blend, then bind, and the pair always agrees.

Here is the recipe. Start with two plain 0 qubits. Put an H on qubit 0. Now qubit 0 is a blend. Add a CNOT with qubit 0 as the control and qubit 1 as the target. The control is a blend, so the target is a blend too, and they are tied together.

The state is now half 00 and half 11. If you measure qubit 0 and see 0, qubit 1 will be 0. If you see 1, qubit 1 will be 1. Each coin alone is perfectly random, yet the two always agree. (See Figure 9.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 9.1. A Bell pair: the two results always agree.

items: This cannot be a product state. A product state has a0 times d equal to b times c. Here the amplitudes are 0.7071, 0, 0, 0.7071. The first times the last is 0.5, but the middle two give 0. They do not match, so this state is entangled.

Time for the lab in the practice section. Solve the levels: copy a bit with CNOT, make a Bell pair, make the opposite pair, and build a three-qubit GHZ state. In the Q Console you can type new 3, h 0, cx 0 1, cx 1 2 and explain.

One more myth to bust. Entanglement is not a phone line. If you are far away from your friend and you measure your qubit, you see a random result. It only shows a pattern when you later compare results. That is why it cannot send messages.
Memory trick: Blend, then Bind. Blend one qubit with H, then Bind it to another with CNOT, and you have a Bell pair.

summary: An oracle is a black box that hides a secret function. Deutsch's problem: is the hidden rule constant (same answer for both inputs) or balanced (different answers)? A normal computer must ask twice. A quantum circuit can ask once.

Grover's search finds a marked item in an unsorted list of N items. A normal computer needs about N over 2 tries on average. Grover needs about the square root of N steps. For a million items that is about a thousand steps instead of half a million.
Both use the interference you learned: the oracle marks the answer with a phase, and the other gates make wrong answers cancel and the right one grow.

ELI5. Deutsch asks a secret box one question instead of two. Grover finds a hidden prize by making the right box a little brighter every round, like turning up a dimmer.

Now the real words. Deutsch's problem is to tell whether a hidden rule is constant or balanced. Grover's problem is to search for a marked item. Both mark the answer with a sign flip, then use interference so that the answer grows. A dimmer switch for the right box is the reflection step.
Try it. In the algorithm lab, solve the four levels: two Deutsch circuits and two Grover circuits. Watch the right answer reach 100 percent in the chances.
If you remember one thing: mark it, mirror it, measure it.

Imagine a secret rule that takes a 0 or a 1 and gives back a 0 or a 1. There are four possible rules. Two are constant: always 0 or always 1. Two are balanced: copy the input, or flip it. You must find out which kind it is.

A normal computer must ask the rule twice, once for 0 and once for 1, to compare the answers. Deutsch's circuit asks once. It puts the input in a blend, asks the oracle, and then lets the two paths interfere. If the rule is constant the answer is 0, if balanced the answer is 1.

lesson.code:
def deutsch(f0, f1):
    a0 = ((-1) ** f0 + (-1) ** f1) / 2
    p0 = a0 * a0
    return 'constant' if p0 > 0.5 else 'balanced'
print(deutsch(0, 0), deutsch(0, 1))

items: Grover's search is the more useful one. Take 4 hidden boxes and one of them has a prize. A normal computer checks boxes one at a time. Grover starts with an even blend of all boxes, marks the prize with a phase, and then does a reflection that makes the prized box more likely.
(See Figure 10.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 10.1. Grover on four items: mark the prize, then reflect about the average.

items: For 4 items one round makes the prize certain. For larger lists you repeat the round about pi over 4 times the square root of N times. Do too few rounds and the prize is not yet likely. Do too many and it fades again. It rotates like a clock hand.

lesson.code:
import math
N = 16
k = int(math.pi / 4 * math.sqrt(N))
print('rounds:', k)
theta = math.asin(1 / math.sqrt(N))
print('chance of prize:', round(math.sin((2 * k + 1) * theta) ** 2, 3))

items: Nobody gets to skip checking. Real Grover circuits include an oracle and a flip around the average. The lab gives you ready circuits to experiment with so you can see the answer rise.

summary: Real quantum chips are fragile. Heat, vibration and stray signals disturb qubits and make mistakes. This is noise, and the loss of the quantum blend is called decoherence. Many chips work near absolute zero.

Because one measurement gives one random answer, you run the circuit many times. Each run is a shot. A hundred shots show you the chances roughly, a thousand show more. The error shrinks with the square root of the shots.

A normal computer can simulate a quantum one, but it needs 2 to the n numbers. Around 30 qubits fills a normal PC and around 50 fills a supercomputer. That is exactly why real hardware is interesting.

ELI5. Real quantum computers are shy and wobbly, so we repeat the test many times and count what we see, the way you roll a die often to learn if it is fair.

Now the real words. Each run is a shot. The counts are noisy because chance wobbles, and the wobble shrinks as you take more shots. Real hardware adds noise from imperfect gates, which is why error correction is needed.
Try it. Run 10 shots, then 100, then 1000 on a Bell pair and watch 00 and 11 settle towards 50 and 50. Change the seed to see a different random run.
If you remember one thing: more shots, steadier counts.

When you ran 100 shots earlier, you noticed that the Bell state did not give exactly 50 and 50. That is not a bug. Each shot is one random measurement, like a coin flip, so the totals wobble around the true chances.

How big is the wobble? About the square root of p times one minus p, divided by the square root of shots. For a fair coin and 100 shots that is about 0.05, or 5 percent. For 10,000 shots it is 0.005. To be 10 times more accurate you need 100 times more shots. (See Figure 11.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 11.1. More shots give steadier counts.

lesson.code:
shots = 100
p = 0.5
err = (p * (1 - p) / shots) ** 0.5
print('standard error:', round(err, 3))

items: On real hardware the picture is messier. Gates are not perfect, qubits slowly lose their blend, and measurement can read the wrong answer. Today's machines have dozens to hundreds of noisy qubits, and engineers are working on error correction.

Error correction spreads one reliable qubit across many noisy ones, similar to how you repeat a message three times so one smudge does not matter. It is a big engineering goal, and useful big machines need it.

Finally, why a simulator is limited. Every qubit you add doubles the memory. At 16 bytes per number, 30 qubits need 16 gigabytes. 40 qubits need 16 terabytes. That is why a simulator like our lab is great for learning on small circuits, but real chips are needed for large ones.
Memory trick: Quadruple the shots, halve the wobble. Four times as many shots makes the wobble half as big.

summary: OpenQASM stands for Open Quantum Assembly Language. It writes a circuit as plain lines of text, one gate per line. IBM Quantum Composer, Qiskit and many other tools can read and write it.
A program has a header, a place to declare qubits, a list of gates and a measurement. Every line ends with a semicolon. Comments start with two slashes.
Version 3 is the modern one and the composer shows it. Older files use version 2, with slightly different words, and you can convert them by hand.

ELI5. OpenQASM is a recipe card for a circuit: one line for each move, written in a language every quantum machine can read. You can mail it to a friend and they can run your exact circuit.

Now the real words. The first line names the version. Then you declare how many qubits you have. Then each gate is one line, such as h q[0]; and cx q[0], q[1];. Version 2 and version 3 look a little different but mean the same thing.
Try it. Open the lab, build H then CNOT, and read the OpenQASM tab. Change a line of the text and press Apply to see the picture change.
If you remember one thing: name it, size it, use it: version, qubits, gates.

Think of OpenQASM as the recipe card for a circuit. The picture in the composer and the card say exactly the same thing. The advantage of text is that you can save it, mail it, paste it into other tools or run it on a real machine. (See Figure 12.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 12.1. The same Bell circuit as a picture and as OpenQASM.

items: Our lab reads micro QASM, a small friendly slice of OpenQASM 2 and 3: qubit declarations, the standard gates, angles like pi/2 and measure. If you use something it does not support, such as loops or custom gates, it tells you the line and what to change.

Read it top down. The first line names the version. The include line brings in the standard gates, so h, x and cx mean what you expect. The qubit line makes two qubits called q, numbered from 0. The bit line makes two classical bits called c to hold the answers.

Then come the gates, one per line, in the order they happen. A gate name, a space, then the qubits it acts on. h q[0]; is an H on qubit 0. cx q[0], q[1]; is a CNOT with qubit 0 as control and qubit 1 as target. The last line measures every qubit into the bits.

Here is how our composer symbols map to the text. H is h, X is x, Y is y, Z is z, T is t, CNOT is cx and CZ is cz. Each column of the composer becomes a few lines, in order from left to right. Open the Code panel on the OpenQASM tab and watch it change as you tap.

You will meet older version 2 files. They say qreg and creg instead of qubit and bit, include a library called qelib1.inc, and measure with an arrow. The gates are the same. Converting between the two is mostly renaming a few lines.

Version 3 adds extras that you will grow into. You can define your own gate, like a recipe that calls other gates. You can run a gate only if a measured bit is 1, which is how teleportation works. And you can write angles for rotation gates, like rz(pi/4) q[0]; which is a smaller phase turn.
Memory trick: Name it, Size it, Use it. OpenQASM: Name the version, Size the qubits, Use the gates, one per line.

In Qiskit you make a QuantumCircuit and call methods like h, x and cx. A Statevector gives you the exact chances, and a Sampler runs shots on a simulator or a real chip.
Watch one trap: Qiskit counts qubits from 0 and prints qubit 0 on the right, while our composer reads q[0] at the top and writes it on the left.

ELI5. The composer draws your circuit, and the code panel writes the same thing as words, like a drawing and its caption. Qiskit is a way of writing that caption in Python so the computer can run it.

Now the real words. Qiskit is an open source Python toolkit from IBM. You build a QuantumCircuit, add gates with methods like h and cx, transpile it for a chip, run it with a Sampler and read the counts. MicroQiskit in our lab is a tiny version with the same shapes.
Try it. In the Qiskit lab type qc.h(0) and qc.cx(0, 1) in the Python tab and press Run. The circuit appears in the composer. Remember Qiskit writes qubit 0 on the right.
If you remember one thing: build, transpile, run, read.

Open any lab and the Code panel below the composer. Build the Bell state with H then CNOT and open Qiskit. You will see a few lines of Python. The composer did not invent the code. It just translated your picture.

lesson.code:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector

qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)

print(Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict())

items: Line by line. The first line makes a circuit with 2 qubits, both starting at 0. The H puts qubit 0 in a blend. The CNOT links qubit 1 to it. Statevector works out the chances exactly with no shots, like our bars. The output shows 00 and 11 with 0.5 each.

Next is the trap. Our composer reads left to right, so q[0] is the leftmost bit. Qiskit does the opposite and writes qubit 0 on the right. A state we call 10 appears in Qiskit as 01. The result is the same, only the label is flipped, so always check which one you are reading.
(See Figure 13.1 below.)

lesson.caption: Figure 13.1. Our composer puts qubit 0 on the left. Qiskit puts it on the right.

items: OpenQASM is the same circuit as plain text. Many tools can read it, so it works like a shared language. To run on a real chip, you make a free IBM Quantum account, pick a machine, and the toolkit transpiles your circuit into the gates that chip supports. Queues can take a while, so simulate first.

Inside our Quantum Web Lab the Python tab runs MicroQiskit, a tiny Qiskit we wrote that works offline in your browser. It has QuantumCircuit, the same gate methods and simulate. Real Qiskit code looks almost the same, so what you learn here carries over.
The Python you press Run on is turned back into a circuit, so you can go from code to picture and back.
Qiskit and OpenQASM are close friends. Qiskit can write any circuit out as OpenQASM text and read it back in, so the recipe card from the last chapter works as a bridge between tools.
A circuit you drew in the composer, saved as OpenQASM, can be loaded into Qiskit with one line and sent to a real chip.

A full Qiskit program has four steps. Build the circuit. Transpile it, which rewrites it for the gates a chip supports. Run it with a Sampler to get counts. Then read the counts, which look just like the Shots tab: a table of results and how many times each came up. (See Figure 13.2 below.)

A good habit: draw it in the composer, look at the Qiskit code, change one line, and predict what changes. Then try the code in a notebook. Reading code that you drew yourself is a gentle way into real quantum programming.

summary: Quantum computers are expected to help with a few kinds of problems: simulating molecules and materials, searching, and breaking some codes. Shor's algorithm can factor large numbers much faster than known normal methods.

That is why people are building new codes that resist quantum attacks. Everyday tasks like browsing, email, games and spreadsheets will not get faster. Quantum computers are co-processors for special jobs.

To keep going: play with the Quantum Web Lab, try IBM Quantum and other free cloud services, follow Qiskit and Cirq tutorials, and read about the linear algebra under the hood. You already know the key ideas.

items: Quick recap of the last chapter, Qiskit: real quantum code in Python:
• qc = QuantumCircuit(2) makes 2 qubits.
• qc.h(0) is an H on qubit 0. qc.cx(0, 1) is a CNOT.
• Statevector(qc).probabilities_dict() gives exact chances.
• Qiskit prints qubit 0 on the right.
• OpenQASM 3 is the shared text format.
ELI5. Quantum computers will be special helpers for chemistry and secret codes, not faster game consoles. They are more like a telescope than a faster bicycle.

Now the real words. They may help simulate molecules, search without a map, factor big numbers with Shor's algorithm and solve some optimisation problems. They do not try every answer at once, and they will not speed up email or games.
Try it. Look at the figure in this chapter and sort ten jobs into good fit and bad fit. Then pick one topic to try next, such as the Qiskit textbook.
If you remember one thing: a special tool, not a faster everything.

What could a large reliable quantum computer do? The most natural job is simulating nature, because nature is quantum. That might mean better batteries, medicines and fertilizers. A normal computer struggles because the numbers double with every particle. (See Figure 14.1 below.)

items: Shor's algorithm factors a large number into primes. Today's internet security often relies on factoring being hard. A big enough quantum computer would break some of it. The reply is new encryption that quantum computers cannot break, and it is already being rolled out.

The code above factors by trying every divisor. It is fine for small numbers and hopeless for numbers hundreds of digits long. Shor's trick is to find a repeating pattern using interference, and from the pattern it works out the factors.
Common myths. A quantum computer does not try every answer at once and pick the best. It is not a faster laptop. It cannot send messages faster than light. And it is not here to replace your phone.

You now know qubits, amplitudes, gates, interference, entanglement and a little of two algorithms. Keep playing. Build a circuit, guess the result before you run it, and see if you were right. That is how real quantum programmers learn.
